answers.answer: A caller supplies a key to retrieve its associated value. Use a consistently escaped tuple of tenant ID, device ID, and record kind settings (distinct from status); the value is the complete device-settings record. Tenant distinguishes repeated device IDs; record kind distinguishes settings from status. This is authoritative because the application treats it as source of truth, not necessarily a disposable cache. Key-value access alone promises no crash survival: verify persistence and failure guarantees. With replacement puts, the second put removes color, so get returns {mode: loud}; after delete, a read observing the deletion reports absence. A get timeout confirms neither presence nor absence because no result arrived. Verify caller access to the tenant and device record; knowing or guessing its key is not authorization.

evidence.quote: Identifies an entry within a store or namespace. The caller supplies this identifier to find the associated value.

A key-value store can hold authoritative data, the record the application treats as its source of truth. It can also hold a disposable copy of data kept elsewhere. That second role is caching; the access model does not decide the role.
The key-value label says nothing by itself about whether acknowledged writes survive a crash. Check the store's persistence settings and failure guarantees before using it as the only copy.
Use an unambiguous encoding of those parts. A separator is safe only if values cannot contain it or are escaped consistently. Every caller must construct the same identity the same way.
A key selects data; it does not grant permission. Verify the caller's access to the organization and record before reading or changing it. A guessed key must not bypass that check.
Stores a value at a key. In a replacement API, putting {mode: quiet, color: green}, then {mode: loud}, leaves only {mode: loud}. The old color field is gone.
Removes the entry. A subsequent read that observes this deletion reports absence.

A get timeout means no result arrived. It does not tell you whether the key exists. Keep operational failures separate from confirmed absence; turning an outage into 'not found' can create incorrect replacement data.

answers.answer: Basic lookup requires equipment IDs; embedding region in a value does not provide a way to discover all west IDs efficiently. A scan reads entries and filters their values; work grows with entries inspected even if few match. A region-to-IDs index locates candidate IDs without reading every value, then fetches their records. It costs storage and update work: region changes and deletions must update the index too. Check who maintains it and when updates become visible; application maintenance adds coordination. Index support cannot be assumed for every key-value store.

evidence.quote: Knowing a record's ID lets you fetch it. Asking for all records in a city is a different operation when you do not know their IDs. Storing the city inside each value does not create an efficient lookup by city.
Examines entries and filters their values. Its work grows with the entries inspected, even if few match. Filtering the results does not undo the reads already performed.
Maintains another lookup, such as city to matching record IDs. It can find candidates without inspecting every value, then fetch the needed records.

An index takes storage and update work. When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too. Check who maintains it and when its results reflect writes; an application-maintained index adds coordination work.
Some stores supply indexes or ordered range queries; basic key-value access promises neither. Choose the actual access path for each required query.

answers.answer: Both blind writes store 21, leaving 21 instead of the intended 22: one increment is lost. With atomic version checking, the first worker conditionally replaces 20/version 7 with 21 and an advanced version. The second worker’s expected version 7 no longer matches, so its stale write is rejected. It rereads 21 and the current version, recomputes 22, and conditionally attempts that change; if no further conflict occurs it succeeds and advances the version again. Bound retries under continuing contention. A separate check can pass for both before either write, so an unconditional put after it still has the race. The lesson does not specify the exact version-number advancement rule.

evidence.quote: Two callers read a count of 10. Each adds one locally and puts 11. Both writes can succeed, but the final count is 11 instead of 12. One intended increment is lost.

Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation. With version checking, a caller supplies the version it read; the store writes only if that version still matches, and advances it on success.

Only one update based on the old version succeeds. The rejected caller rereads the current value and version, recomputes its change and makes another conditional attempt. Bound retries when contention persists.

Checking the version in a separate request before an unconditional put leaves the same race. Verify that the chosen store supports the required atomic operation. Protection for one key does not automatically cover a group of keys or an external action.

answers.answer: A timeout leaves execution unknown: the write may have finished and only its response was lost. Repeating the identical replacement leaves the same value if no other write intervenes; repeating an increment adds again if the first ran, even when each increment is atomic. Duplicate prevention requires recognizing the same logical operation with the same ID and intent on retries, atomically coordinating its recorded identity and data change, and retaining duplicate records for the retry window. Verify actual product support and scope; an ID alone is insufficient. Without verified protection, reconcile the uncertain increment through application recovery rather than blindly repeat it; the lesson gives no concrete recovery implementation. TTL is expiration; eviction removes data for capacity pressure and may happen before TTL. TTL therefore guarantees neither retention until the deadline, refresh after removal, nor exact-deadline business execution. A cache can reload from its source; authoritative data needs deliberate retention/recovery. Enforce access deadlines during authorization and use an appropriate execution mechanism for timed work. Check product TTL support, when expired data stops being readable versus physical deletion, eviction policy/configuration, and retry/duplicate-protection behavior.

evidence.quote: A write can finish and its reply can be lost. A timeout therefore does not prove that the write failed to execute.

Repeating the same operation leaves the same result. Replacing a value with the identical value twice does this if no other write intervenes. Executing an increment twice adds twice, even if each increment is individually atomic.

To prevent duplicate increments, the system must recognize the same logical operation and prevent a second effect. Keep the same ID and intent on retries. A request ID alone is insufficient: recording it and changing the data must be coordinated atomically, with duplicate records retained for the retry window. Verify the product's actual support and scope.

Without verified duplicate protection, do not blindly repeat the uncertain increment. Reconcile its outcome through an application recovery path. Use bounded retry/backoff for retryable failures; retrying every error can worsen an outage.

An expiration rule for an entry. Check when the product stops returning expired data and when it physically removes it. For example, DynamoDB's background TTL deletion can leave expired items readable while deletion is pending.
Removes entries to manage capacity, such as memory pressure, when the store's policy permits it. An entry can disappear before its TTL; a TTL is not a promise to retain it until the deadline.

Neither removal mechanism fetches a fresh replacement. A cache user may reload from its source; an authoritative record needs a deliberate retention and recovery policy. Do not silently treat required data as disposable.

Expiration is also not a scheduler promising that business work runs at the exact deadline. Enforce an access deadline when authorizing use, and use a suitable work-execution mechanism for timed actions.
Check TTL support, expiry visibility and eviction configuration in the chosen implementation before relying on any of them.

answers.answer: A partition is a portion of the keyspace assigned to a node or group. Distributing different key groups spreads storage and request work across many keys. When most requests hit one key, its serving capacity can remain the bottleneck despite more partitions; measure request distribution, not merely key count. A lagging replica returning an older value is a read-visibility/consistency issue. Durability concerns acknowledged data surviving specified failures: a durable write can be missing from a lagging read, and seeing a new value does not prove crash survival. Before promising latest reads or acknowledged-write survival, verify the implementation, persistence and replication settings, chosen read/write mode and its freshness/failure guarantees. The lesson supplies no product-specific guarantee for this store.

evidence.quote: A portion of the keyspace assigned to a storage node or group. Distributing different key groups can spread their storage and request work.

Receives a disproportionate share of requests. More partitions alone may not help when most work still targets that key's serving capacity. Measure the distribution of requests, not just the number of keys.

Describes which writes a read is guaranteed to observe. A replica is another maintained copy; if it lags and the read mode permits stale results, it can return an older value after a successful write.
Concerns whether acknowledged data survives specified failures. A durable write can still be absent from a lagging read. Conversely, seeing a new value does not prove that it will survive a crash.

Check the implementation, persistence and replication settings, and the selected read/write mode. More nodes or a successful acknowledgement alone cannot establish every freshness and failure-survival guarantee.

answers.answer: A directly fits basic key-value access: its known account key locates the complete independent preferences without scanning to discover matches. B’s frequent joins and changing field filters need additional access paths: scans read extra data, indexes require update work, and application-side joins add requests and coordination. Richer queries or transactions may fit B better. For A I would verify authorization so a known or guessed account key cannot expose another account’s preferences, and concurrent-update support so overlapping preference changes can use an atomic version condition rather than silently overwrite each other. The access model alone proves neither speed nor safety: value size, network, hot keys and implementation limits still affect performance, and required correctness guarantees must be verified. Measure representative requests and failures; no measured performance is supplied here.

evidence.quote: Independent records fetched and replaced by a known key are a direct fit. The application can ask for the needed value without discovering matching records through a scan.

Joins combine related records. Frequent joins or new filters over value fields need more than basic key lookup. Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.
A store with richer query or transaction support may fit those requirements better. A product can support several access models; the labels alone do not decide the choice.
A key selects data; it does not grant permission. Verify the caller's access to the organization and record before reading or changing it. A guessed key must not bypass that check.

Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation. With version checking, a caller supplies the version it read; the store writes only if that version still matches, and advances it on success.

Before selecting it, verify authorization, value size and traffic distribution, concurrent-update and retry behavior, required read freshness, durability and retention. Explain which requirements matter for this workload and what happens when the store is unavailable.
Measure representative requests and failures. A known-key lookup can avoid unnecessary search, but network, value size, hot keys and implementation limits still affect latency and capacity.
